transcript.text: indesit oven stoped heating, fan goes round n light on but its stone cold after 20 mins. grill werks fine tho. any ideas b4 i call some1 out

This is a very common issue with Indesit (and many other brands) electric ovens. The fact that the grill works and the fan/light work gives us a huge clue: your mains power supply to the oven is fine, so the problem is isolated to the specific heating element for baking.

Here are the most likely causes, ranked from most common/easiest to fix to more serious issues:

### 1. The Bake Element Has Failed (Most Likely)
The circular element at the back of your oven (the "bake" element) has likely burned out or developed an internal break in the heating coil.
• Why it fits: If this element fails, the fan will still run (to circulate air), the light works, and the grill (which is a separate element at the top) still works perfectly. But no heat is generated for baking.
• How to check:
• Unplug the oven or switch off the circuit breaker.
• Look at the back element. Do you see any obvious cracks, blisters, or holes in the metal coil? Sometimes it’s visible.
• If you have a multimeter, set it to continuity/resistance (Ohms). Remove the two screws holding the element in place, pull it out gently (don’t stretch the wires!), and test the terminals. A good element usually reads between 20–30 Ohms. If it reads "OL" or infinity, it’s dead.
• Fix: Replace the bake element. They are cheap (£15–£30) and easy to swap (usually just 2 screws).

### 2. Loose Wiring at the Element Terminals
Sometimes the element itself is fine, but the wires connecting to it have come loose or burnt out due to heat cycling.
• How to check: With power OFF, inspect the two terminals where the wires connect to the back of the bake element. Are they blackened? Loose? Broken off?
• Fix: Tighten connections or replace the terminal block if damaged.

### 3. Faulty Oven Thermostat or Temperature Sensor
If the element is working but not heating, it could be that the oven’s "brain" isn’t sending power to it because it thinks the oven is already hot (even though it’s cold).
• How to check: This is harder to diagnose without a multimeter and technical knowledge. You’d need to test the sensor’s resistance at room temperature vs. when heated.
• Likelihood: Less common than a failed element, but possible on older models.

### 4. Faulty Relay on the Control Board
The electronic control board has relays that switch power to different elements (grill, bake, fan). If the relay for the bake circuit is stuck open or dead, no power reaches the element.
• How to check: You might hear a faint "click" from the back of the oven when you turn on the bake function. No click might indicate a board issue. However, this is less common than element failure.

---

### ✅ What You Should Do Before Calling Someone Out:

1.  Do a visual inspection: Look at the back bake element for obvious damage.
2.  Test the element (if comfortable): If you have basic DIY skills and a multimeter, test for continuity. This is the #1 thing technicians will do anyway.
3.  Check for error codes: Some Indesit models flash lights or show codes if there’s a fault. Consult your manual.
4.  Reset the oven: Unplug it from the wall (or switch off the breaker) for 5–10 minutes, then plug it back in. This can sometimes reset a glitchy control board.

### ⚠️ Safety Warning:
• Always disconnect power before inspecting or touching any internal components.
• If you are not comfortable using a multimeter or opening the oven panel, do not attempt to fix it yourself. Gas and electric appliances can be dangerous if mishandled.

### 💡 Cost-Saving Tip:
If the bake element is dead (which is 90% likely), replacing it yourself costs ~£20 for the part and takes 15 minutes. A technician call-out alone could cost £60–£80, plus labor. If you’re handy, this is a great DIY job.

Summary: Your oven’s bake element has most likely failed. Check it first!

its hardwired not a plug, but theres a cooker switch on the wall n i know where it is so can isolate it. ill have a look at the back element. dont have a multimeter tho, any other way to tell if its the element?

Since you don’t have a multimeter, we’ll rely on visual inspection and process of elimination. Here’s how to safely check:

### 1. Visual Inspection (The "Blinker" Test)
• Safety First: Ensure the cooker switch is OFF before touching anything inside.
• Look closely at the bake element (the circular one at the back). Do you see any obvious cracks, holes, or blisters in the metal coil? If yes, it’s dead.
• Turn the cooker switch ON and set a baking temperature (e.g., 180°C). Watch the element for 2–3 minutes. Does it glow red/orange at all? Even a faint glow means it has some life left. If it stays completely dark while the fan runs, the element is likely dead.

### 2. Check for Loose Connections
• With power OFF again, remove the two screws holding the bake element in place. Gently pull the element forward just enough to see the terminals (the metal tabs where the wires connect).
• Look for:
• Blackened or burnt plastic around the terminals.
• Wires that look loose, frayed, or disconnected.
• Corrosion or white/green buildup.
• If anything looks damaged here, that’s your culprit.

### 3. The "Grill vs. Bake" Clue
You mentioned the grill works fine. This confirms:
• Your mains power is reaching the oven.
• The main control board is likely getting basic signals.
• It isolates the fault to either the bake element itself, its wiring, or the relay/thermostat controlling that specific circuit.

### Next Steps if Visual Checks Show Nothing:
If the element looks perfect and connections are tight, but it still doesn’t heat, the issue is likely internal (a failed relay on the control board or a faulty thermostat). At this point, since you’re not using a multimeter to test continuity, it’s best to call out a qualified engineer. They’ll use a multimeter to quickly confirm if power is reaching the element terminals when the oven is set to bake.

Summary:
1. Isolate power.
2. Check for visible damage on the back element.
3. Tighten any loose terminal connections.
4. If no obvious issues, replace the bake element (it’s cheap and easy). If that doesn’t work, call an engineer.
isolated it n took the back panel off. theres a blister/split in the coil near the bottom with a black mark on it. so thats the element then?

Yes, that’s definitely your problem. The blister and split mean the heating coil has broken internally, so no current can flow through it to generate heat. The black mark is likely carbon buildup from arcing at the break point.

### How to Replace It:
1. Buy the Right Part: Note down the model number of your Indesit oven (usually on a sticker inside the door frame or on the back). Search for "Indesit [model] bake element" or "oven heating element." Generic elements often fit multiple models, but it’s worth checking compatibility.
2. Disconnect Wires: With power still OFF, unscrew the two nuts/bolts holding the wires to the terminals at the back of the oven wall (where the element connects). Take a photo first so you know which wire goes where.
3. Remove Old Element: Unscrew the two screws holding the element to the back panel and carefully pull it out.
4. Install New Element: Position the new element, screw it in place, and reconnect the wires exactly as they were. Double-check that connections are tight.
5. Test: Replace the back panel, restore power, and test the oven on a baking setting.

It’s a straightforward DIY job if you’re comfortable with basic tools and electrical safety. Let me know if you need help finding the part number!
ok thanks, model is IFW 6330 IX off the door frame plate. also heard a little pop from the back last time it worked, if that matters. ill order the element, anything else i should check b4 i fit it?

The "pop" you heard was almost certainly the heating coil snapping internally as it failed. That confirms the element is definitely dead and needs replacing.

Before you fit the new one, here are a few things to check:

1. Inspect the Terminals: Look at the two metal terminals on the oven wall where the wires connect. If they’re blackened, melted, or pitted from the "pop," clean them with fine sandpaper or replace them if damaged. Poor connections can cause new elements to fail prematurely.
2. Check Wire Insulation: Follow the wires back a few inches from the terminals. Look for any signs of heat damage, melting, or brittleness. If the insulation is cracked or flaking, those wires may need replacing too.
3. Verify the Model Number: Double-check that IFW 6330 IX is correct. Sometimes there’s a suffix (like -1 or A) that matters for part compatibility. When ordering, search for "Indesit IFW6330IX bake element" or "oven heating element."
4. Clean the Oven: While you’re in there, it’s a good time to wipe down any grease or debris from the back panel. This helps prevent future issues and keeps things running smoothly.

Once you’ve checked those points, fitting the new element should be straightforward. Let me know if you need help with anything else!
